blocks.text: Say you have two arrays of prices and you want to apply a discount, or you have a batch of neural network activations and you need to squash every single number into a probability. Both jobs come down to the same core skill: running a math operation across every element of an array at once, without writing a single loop. This is the beating heart of NumPy, and honestly, once it clicks, plain Python loops over lists start to feel painfully slow and clunky by comparison.

blocks.caption: Same shape in, same shape out, added position by position.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441815215-760144912.png
1. Introduction

This lesson covers the elementwise mathematical toolkit in NumPy: the arithmetic operators, the common math functions like square root and exponential, trigonometric functions, comparison operators, and the sharp edges around floating point precision. Everything here happens elementwise, meaning the operation is applied independently to each number in the array, position by position.

Two topics that sound related are deliberately left out of this lesson. Statistical operations like mean, sum, and standard deviation get their own dedicated lesson, because those operations collapse an array down into fewer numbers rather than working elementwise. Linear algebra operations like matrix multiplication and the dot product also get their own dedicated lesson, because they combine numbers across positions rather than one at a time. This lesson touches matrix multiplication only briefly, just enough to help you tell it apart from elementwise multiplication.

blocks.title: Why this matters for ML/AI work
blocks.content: Every activation function, every normalization step, every loss calculation you will ever write starts with elementwise math. A sigmoid, a ReLU, a min max scaler, a gradient update, they are all built from the operators and functions in this lesson stacked together.

blocks.text: 2. Arithmetic Operators on Arrays

NumPy overloads the standard Python arithmetic operators so that they work directly on arrays. When you apply one of these operators to two arrays of the same shape, NumPy lines them up position by position and applies the operator to each matching pair.

Every one of these runs elementwise. The first element of a only ever interacts with the first element of b, the second only with the second, and so on. There is no mixing across positions, which is exactly what makes the operation predictable and fast.

blocks.caption: Multiplication lines up the same way addition does, position by position.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441815215-581107658.png

Each of these operators also has a function form, and the two are completely interchangeable. Reaching for the function form is mostly useful when you are building something generic, like a list of operations to apply in a loop, where you need to pass the operation itself around as a value rather than writing it inline.

blocks.title: A quiet detail about division
blocks.content: Regular division with / always returns floats in NumPy, even if both arrays only contain integers. So an integer array divided by another integer array still comes back as a float array, which is exactly what you want for most ML math, since you rarely want division silently truncated to whole numbers.

blocks.text: 2.1 Power, Floor Division, and Modulo
Three more operators round out the arithmetic set, and they show up constantly in feature engineering and loss functions.

items: The double star operator raises each element to a power, so a ** 2 squares every value in the array in one shot.
The double slash operator does floor division, dividing and then rounding down to the nearest whole number for each element.
The percent operator returns the remainder of dividing each element, which is handy for things like checking even or odd, or wrapping an index around a fixed range.

blocks.caption: Power and floor division are two more elementwise operators worth knowing by heart.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441815216-375200058.png
2.2 Operating an Array Against a Scalar

You do not need two arrays for this to work. NumPy will happily apply an operator between an entire array and a single scalar, stretching that scalar across every position through a mechanism called broadcasting. If you want the full story on broadcasting rules for mismatched shapes, that gets its own dedicated lesson, but the simple scalar case is worth seeing here.

code.content:
prices = np.array([100, 250, 80, 400])
discounted = prices * 0.8   # apply a 20 percent discount to every price at once
print(discounted)            # [ 80. 200.  64. 320.]

blocks.alt: Operating an Array Against a Scalar
blocks.caption: A scalar gets applied to every element without you writing a loop.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441815216-189227673.png

This single line replaces a for loop that would otherwise iterate over every price, multiply it, and stuff the result into a new list. The array version is shorter to write and runs dramatically faster once the arrays get large, because NumPy pushes the loop down into optimized C code instead of running it in slow interpreted Python.
3. Common Elementwise Math Functions

Beyond the basic operators, NumPy ships a whole family of math functions that also apply elementwise. These are the functions you will reach for constantly once you start writing anything resembling machine learning code.

blocks.caption: Four of the most used elementwise math functions, all fed from the same input array.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441815216-81785949.png

Notice that every single one of these takes an array in and returns an array of the exact same shape out. That shape preserving behavior is a hallmark of elementwise operations, and it is a good sanity check whenever you are unsure whether something is elementwise or not: if the output shape matches the input shape, it almost certainly ran elementwise.

np.abs deserves a special mention because of how often it shows up in evaluating models. Mean absolute error, one of the most common regression metrics, is nothing more than np.abs applied to the difference between predictions and true values, followed by an average. You will see that exact pattern again once you reach the statistical operations lesson.

code.content:
predictions = np.array([3.1, 5.9, 2.0])
actuals = np.array([3.0, 6.0, 2.5])

errors = np.abs(predictions - actuals)
print(errors)   # [0.1 0.1 0.5]

blocks.text: 3.1 A Quick Word on Trigonometric Functions
NumPy also has the standard trig functions, np.sin and np.cos, and they behave exactly like the other math functions above, applying to each element independently.

You might not reach for these every day, but they show up in two places worth knowing about. Transformer models use sine and cosine together to build positional encodings, giving each token position a unique wave pattern the model can learn to interpret. Signal processing pipelines, like anything dealing with audio, sensor readings, or time series, also lean heavily on sine and cosine to model periodic behavior.
4. Comparison Operators and Boolean Arrays

Comparison operators like greater than, less than, and equals also apply elementwise on arrays, and instead of returning a single true or false, they return a whole new array of boolean values, one for each position.

code.content:
scores = np.array([55, 82, 91, 40, 67])

print(scores > 60)    # [False  True  True False  True]
print(scores < 50)    # [ True False False  True False]
print(scores == 82)   # [False  True False False False]

blocks.caption: Every comparison operator on arrays returns a full boolean array, not a single answer.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441815216-197729955.png

This boolean array is genuinely useful on its own. It becomes a mask you can use to filter, count, or select values, a pattern you will see everywhere once you get to boolean masking and fancy indexing later in this course.
4.1 The Equals Trap: == Does Not Work Like Python Lists

This is the single most common beginner mistake with NumPy comparisons, so it deserves its own section. In plain Python, comparing two lists with == checks whether the whole lists are equal and gives you back one true or false answer. Comparing two NumPy arrays with == does something completely different: it compares elementwise and hands you back an entire array of results.

code.content:
python_list_a = [1, 2, 3]
python_list_b = [1, 2, 3]
print(python_list_a == python_list_b)   # True, one single answer

array_a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
array_b = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(array_a == array_b)   # [ True  True  True], three separate answers

blocks.alt: The Equals Trap: == Does Not Work Like Python Lists
blocks.caption: The classic trap: array equals array gives you an array back, not a single yes or no.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441815216-224036231.png

blocks.title: The trap in practice
blocks.content: Writing "if array_a == array_b:" inside an if statement will crash with an error about the truth value of an array being ambiguous, because Python does not know how to treat a whole array of true and false values as one single condition. This confuses almost everyone the first time they hit it.

blocks.text: When you actually want one single true or false answer for whether two whole arrays are identical, use np.array_equal instead. It checks both the shape and every value, and returns exactly one boolean.

code.content:
print(np.array_equal(array_a, array_b))   # True, a single answer this time

array_c = np.array([1, 2, 4])
print(np.array_equal(array_a, array_c))   # False

blocks.alt: The Equals Trap: == Does Not Work Like Python Lists
blocks.caption: np.array_equal is the correct tool whenever you want one answer for the whole array.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441815417-320657891.png
5. Elementwise Multiplication Versus Matrix Multiplication

This distinction trips up a huge number of people coming from a math background, and it is worth being crystal clear about it here even though the deep dive lives in the dedicated linear algebra lesson. The star operator between two arrays always multiplies elementwise, matching each position independently. The at operator, along with np.dot and np.matmul, computes an actual matrix multiplication, combining rows and columns together through sums of products.

code.content:
m1 = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
m2 = np.array([[5, 6], [7, 8]])

print(m1 * m2)        # elementwise: [[ 5 12] [21 32]]
print(m1 @ m2)        # matrix multiply: [[19 22] [43 50]]
print(np.matmul(m1, m2))   # same result as m1 @ m2

blocks.caption: Same two arrays, two completely different operators, two completely different answers.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441815418-305654782.png

blocks.title: Keep them mentally separate
blocks.content: The star operator never sums anything across positions, it simply multiplies matching cells. The at operator and np.matmul sum products across a shared dimension, which is exactly what makes matrix multiplication so central to how neural network layers transform data. Full coverage of that mechanics lives in the linear algebra lesson.

blocks.text: 6. Floating Point Precision Gotchas

Floating point numbers cannot represent every decimal value exactly, because computers store them in binary, and plenty of ordinary decimal fractions simply do not have a clean binary equivalent. This is not a NumPy quirk, it is how floating point math works everywhere, in every language, but it becomes a real problem the moment you compare two floats with ==.

code.content:
print(0.1 + 0.2)          # 0.30000000000000004
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)    # False, even though it looks like it should be True

blocks.caption: A tiny rounding error is enough to make a perfectly reasonable equals check fail.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441815418-994333373.png

This gotcha is everywhere in ML/AI code, because you are constantly comparing computed floating point results against expected values, whether that is checking if a loss converged, verifying two normalized arrays match, or testing a hand rolled function against a library function. If you rely on == for any of that, you will eventually get burned by a false negative that has nothing to do with your logic being wrong.
6.1 The Fix: np.isclose and np.allclose

NumPy gives you two functions built exactly for this problem. np.isclose compares two values, or two arrays elementwise, and considers them equal as long as they are within a small tolerance of each other, rather than demanding a bit for bit exact match. np.allclose does the same check but collapses the result down into one single true or false for the whole array, similar in spirit to np.array_equal but tolerant of tiny floating point noise.

code.content:
print(np.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))   # True

arr1 = np.array([0.1 + 0.2, 1.0])
arr2 = np.array([0.3, 1.0])
print(np.isclose(arr1, arr2))    # [ True  True]
print(np.allclose(arr1, arr2))   # True

blocks.caption: np.isclose accepts a tiny tolerance instead of demanding a perfect bit for bit match.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441815418-278417226.png

blocks.title: A habit worth building now
blocks.content: Anytime you are about to compare floating point results with ==, in tests, in debugging, in validating a hand written formula, stop and reach for np.isclose or np.allclose instead. It will save you hours of confusion down the line, especially once you start comparing outputs from your own code against library implementations.

blocks.text: 7. Worked Example: A Manual Sigmoid Function

Let us put several pieces from this lesson together into one real calculation: building the sigmoid function from scratch using nothing but elementwise operations. Sigmoid squashes any real number down into a value between 0 and 1, which is exactly why it shows up as an activation function and as the final step in binary classification models.

The formula is one over one plus e to the power of negative z, where z is whatever input value or array you feed in. Every single step of that formula is something you already know how to do elementwise.

blocks.alt: Worked Example: A Manual Sigmoid Function
blocks.caption: Every single stage of the sigmoid formula is an elementwise operation you already know.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441815418-73569616.png

Walk through what actually happens to each number. Negative z flips the sign of every element. np.exp raises e to the power of each of those negated values. Adding 1 bumps every element up by one flat amount, which is the array plus scalar pattern from earlier in this lesson. Dividing 1 by that whole array runs one final elementwise division. Not a single loop was written, and the function works identically whether z is one number or an array of a million numbers.

items: A large negative input produces a sigmoid output very close to 0.
An input of exactly 0 produces exactly 0.5, the midpoint of the curve.
A large positive input produces a sigmoid output very close to 1.

blocks.title: Checking your own implementation
blocks.content: If you ever want to confirm a hand rolled function like this one matches a trusted library implementation, this is precisely the situation where you compare with np.allclose rather than ==, since both versions will differ in the tiniest decimal places due to floating point rounding.

code.content:
from scipy.special import expit   # scipy's built in sigmoid

reference = expit(z)
print(np.allclose(sigmoid(z), reference))   # True

blocks.text: 8. Recap

Elementwise arithmetic operators, from plus and minus through power and modulo, apply independently to each matching pair of positions across two arrays, or between an array and a scalar. The elementwise math function family, sqrt, exp, log, abs, power, and round, follow the exact same shape preserving pattern, and trig functions like sin and cos join that same family for periodic and positional work.

Comparison operators return a full boolean array rather than one single answer, and == on two arrays is elementwise, not a whole array equality check, use np.array_equal when you want one answer. Elementwise multiplication with the star operator is a completely different operation from matrix multiplication with the at operator or np.matmul. And whenever floating point results are involved, reach for np.isclose or np.allclose instead of ==, because tiny rounding errors are baked into how computers represent decimals.

items: Elementwise arithmetic: plus, minus, times, divide, power, floor divide, modulo.
Elementwise math functions: sqrt, exp, log, abs, power, round, sin, cos.
Comparisons return boolean arrays; use np.array_equal for one true or false answer.
Star multiplies elementwise; at or np.matmul multiplies matrices, covered fully in the linear algebra lesson.
Use np.isclose or np.allclose instead of == whenever floats are involved.
